### 7.4.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of modern digital literacy is frequently trapped in a technocentric fallacy that views human beings merely as terminal operators or passive consumers of digital interfaces (Weizenbaum, 1976; Dreyfus, 1972). From the era of the fourth industrial revolution to the dawn of generative artificial intelligence dominance, public education regarding technology has focused almost exclusively on procedural competencies: how to operate a device, how to recognize classic phishing links, or how to secure passwords using combinations of special characters (Calo, 2014). This approach, however vital in the context of conventional cybersecurity, has proven thoroughly obsolete when confronting artificial cognitive systems capable of hacking not computer code, but the emotional structures and subconscious decision-making processes of human beings (Kahneman, 2011; Reeves & Nass, 1996).
